Agricultural Products Act

maintopic: AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS ACT CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1948

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Usley for an address to His Excellency the Governor General praying that the Agricultural Products Act be continued in force until the thirty-first day of March, one thousand nine hundred and forty-eight.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS ACT CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1948
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us tonight in this debate the Agricultural Products Act which we passed last spring, a resolution to extend it for three months, statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) which was made yesterday at the opening of the house and the address of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) as made this afternoon. Regardless of what may have been said since then in this debate, the whole question before us-and the only question-is the contracts with Britain for the sale of certain agricultural products. I wish, first, to deal briefly with the Prime Minister's statement of yesterday, then, equally briefly with some comments made by the Minister of Agriculture, and, finally, with the merits of the resolution that is before us.
The Prime Minister's statement yesterday told us exactly nothing with respect to the definite prices to be paid and the definite amounts to be delivered under these contracts; and, as far as the country is concerned, that is the major matter they wanted to hear about. In that respect the statement was an empty one, as empty as any that I or this house have ever heard. After three weeks' deliberations by a large mission from the United Kingdom and representatives of the government of Canada, the only definite things in their report with respect to those particular matters are that they agreed not to agree, that they would announce certain prices after we are gone, and that they would carry on the present contracts for a period of three months and wait and see what would happen in the meantime. In my judgment the Prime Minister's statement was nothing more or less than a facesaving device made for the purpose of giving both governments a graceful exit from discussions that had been embarrassing to Canada and not fruitful to the United Kingdom.
Let me now refer briefly to two or three things in that announcement. The Prime Minister stated, and I use his exact words, that agreement had been reached on all matters under review. I want to ask this question. Does the Prime Minister mean to suggest that in those three weeks' deliberations
the question of prices in those contracts and the question of amounts to be delivered were not under review? That is what his statement means. Yet that is what they met here to do. What are we to conclude when the Prime Minister says they agreed on everything that was under review.
The Prime Minister further stated that they had agreed to the continuance of the wheat agreement. Mr. Speaker, they did not need to do that. In the wheat agreement itself it is provided that it shall continue until 1950. There was no need to discuss it at all-no need unless somebody wanted to change it or to get out of carrying it out.
Then the Prime Minister made one other statement. He said they had decided upon the continuance and the renewal of the contracts for livestock products at prices adjusted accordingly. That is a most vague statement. I suggest that if it means that those prices were to be adjusted on the basis of the increased costs of production, it will never be carried out. I suggest, further, that farmers hearing that interpretation of his statement will be disappointed.
I come now to the remarks of the Minister of Agriculture. He discussed, among other things, the question of hog production, whether or not there is a world price for wheat, the price Britain is paying to New Zealand and Australia for certain livestock products and the question of aid to Britain. I wish to make brief comment on each of those four points.
In dealing with hog production, the Minister of Agriculture said that not many farmers were growing little pigs for sale. With all deference, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that that is not the question before us. The question before us and before them is whether it is worth while, as a business proposition, for farmers just now to grow little pigs and feed them to maturity. That is the question which is facing them and facing us. The minister read a letter from a fellow traveller who suggested that he was going to trust in God and Gardiner. I can only say that it is a good thing that farmers still have some faith in God, because most of them have lost both faith and hope in Gardiner even getting prices for them that will keep up with the rapidly increasing costs of production.

maintopic: AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS ACT CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1948
speechtext:
Then the Minister of Agriculture touched on the question of whether or not there is a world price for wheat. If
Agricultural Products Act

he has any doubt about that I suggest that he read the wheat contract which he signed on behalf of this government with the United Kingdom government in connection with that matter. Here is what the contract says:
In determining the price for these two crop years, 1948-49 and 1949-50, the United Kingdom government will have regard to any difference between the prices paid under this agreement in 1946-47 and 1947-48 crop years and the world prices for wheat in 1946-47 and 1947-48 crop years.
That is in the agreement which the minister himself signed on behalf of this government and which a British minister signed on behalf of Britain. If one wants further evidence as to whether or not there is a world price, the minister and other hon. members should look up the daily reports of the wheat board, in which the figure is given at which Canadian wheat other than that in the British market is sold; and during the period of this wheat contract so far, the figure has varied all the way from $2.05 to $3.37. That is the government's own attitude with respect to the question as to whether or not there is a world wheat price.
I am not going to quarrel with the minister as to whether that figure is called a world price or not. The fact is that our wheat is being sold today in the world at more than $3.30 a bushel. The only question we are concerned with, and the only question the Canadian farmers are concerned with, is whether under these circumstances $1.55 a bushel-the price in the British contract-is enough for two-thirds of our crop to be sold for.
The third point I wish to make in connection with the minister's discussion of wheat is this. The resolution before us and the act before us do not deal with wheat at all. There is nothing in the act about wheat. This measure deals with bacon, beef, cheese, eggs and other agricultural products but it does not refer to wheat at all. Whatever has been done in connection with wheat has been done under another act altogether. A discussion on wheat was not proper under this resolution at all. I shall discuss that item in the proper place.
Then the minister referred to the price that Britain is paying in New Zealand and Australia for certain livestock products. I suggest that that is entirely beside the point here. They can produce these products in New Zealand and Australia at little more than half our cost here. But I notice that the minister did not refer to prices of livestock in the United States, or to prices Britain had paid to the United States, nor did he refer to our

cost of production here. We could sell these products in the United States at nearly twice what we are getting in selling them to Britain.
Nothing was said in the minister's statement in that regard. The question is not how much Britain pays New Zealand and Australia for beef. The question is whether, under these contracts, producers of livestock products can get a price high enough to keep up with the rising cost of production. As I will show later, the prices that are being paid now in Canada are not adequate for the purpose.
Then the minister closed with an impassioned plea for aid to Britain. There again, I suggest, that is not the issue before the house. Let 'the government or any minister bring in a measure to provide aid to Britain from this nation under any reasonable arrangement, and I venture to say it will be supported by ninety per cent of the members of this house. If that is the issue before us; if that is what the minister wants to do, he would have been better employed in seeing to it that in the Geneva trade agreements the government did not destroy the British preferential system altogether.
There are two issues before the country. One is aid to Britain and the other, a square deal to Canadian farmers. The government and its spokesmen, during recent months, have been endeavouring to confuse these two issues. But there should not be confusion. Let the government bring in any measure for lend-lease or mutual aid, or for a loan for a gift to help rehabilitate Britain, and I imagine it will have nearly unanimous support in this house. But, as I say, that is not the question. The question is whether we shall have a square deal for farmers, whether our hog producers, our beef, cheese, apple producers, our dairy producers and others are to get prices that will keep them in business under conditions where costs of 'production have been going up faster than prices. That is the question we are dealing with here tonight, and nothing else.
I come now to the merits of the act we are discussing, and the resolution which would seek to have it extended. The motion before us is for the extension of the Agricultural Products Act. That act, I suggest, is improperly named. It should have been named the farm prices reduction act, because that is what it is accomplishing. In any event, that act now terminates on December 31 and the motion asks for its extension to March 31 next.
The act itself, as passed last year, gave to the government a blank cheque to dispose of

Agricultural Products Act
Canadian farm products by contract to governments of other countries. Let me read what clause 3(a) of that act says:
Subject to any regulations that may be made by the governor in council the minister may
(a) sell or export agricultural products to the government of any country or any agency thereof pursuant to any agreement made by the government of Canada with the government of such country or with such agency and for those purposes may purchase agricultural products and make such arrangements for the purchase, sale or export of agricultural products as he considers necessary or desirable.
The act, it will be seen, gives to the Minister of Agriculture powers of dictatorship over farm products and prices. If he makes bad contracts the farmers have to take the rap. Last year we voted against this bill. If it had been restricted to carrying out the contracts in effect after the war, our vote might have been different. But the minister insisted on blank cheque powers to make further contracts.
We did not like the bill in any event because it put the Minister of Agriculture in a position to suppress all provincial marketing machinery that has been built up over many years. And we did not like it because the powers given to the minister were so unlimited. The Minister of Agriculture was given power to make every farmer toe the line.
What is the situation today? One contract, we know, stands, and that is the wheat contract. This resolution does not deal with it at all; but since the minister referred to it, let me make one statement. It is a part of the government's program. In the first year, on the basis of existing prices, it took out of the farmers' pockets 8123,000,000 in cash. This year it will take more; and much of next year's crop the government has already agreed to sell for 82 a bushel, even though Australia has sold her crop for 82.72 a bushel and the world price is 83.30 a bushel odd. On top of that, as the minister explained this afternoon, the intrinsic value of our wheat is fifty-six cents a bushel more than that of Australia. Yet the government is selling our wheat at 81.55 a bushel this year and $2 a bushel next year. The government has kept down the price of our wheat and used it as an excuse to keep down prices of all other farm products.
But what about all other government contracts-those relating to bacon, beef, cheese, mutton, lamb and other farm produce? They are the things this act deals with, not wheat.
The first trouble about these contracts lies with the government itself. It made contracts that are bad in relation to the cost of producing these commodities. It then treated the contracts made as not being contracts at all.
The government proceeded to break many of them by failing to supply the products in the amounts agreed to.
From what we have seen, the whole matter of the agreements has been in a state of chaos. The minister has no right to ask for an extension of the act until he tells the house what the present situation is in regard to these contracts and what the government intends to do in the months ahead. We have no more light on the subject now than we had when we came here. In the near future, the government will look at these things and make some revision, we do not know what, with respect to prices and amounts.
The country has been kept in a state of suspense for weeks, and now the government asks for another blank cheque to continue a policy which has thoroughly disillusioned the farmers and thrown the agricultural industry of the country into turmoil. The government's record on this matter does not commend itself to anyone affected by it. I doubt if it commends itself to members sitting behind the government.
Let me point out some pertinent facts about the measure and the government's administration of it. In the first place, the main provisions of the act were ill-conceived. Altogether too wide powers were given the minister. He was given wide powers to make new contracts in any quantities at any prices without any farmer or anybody else knowing what they were to be. He was given wide powers to seize farm products to fill these contracts and he exercised these powers to the extent he desired. He sold our farm products for less than they can be produced for.
In the second place, the basis of the act was unsound. It was falsely called by the government a stability program for agriculture; but it was based on instability and it was bound to fail. The government called it a stability program, but based it on sales to Britain, which could not pay us for much of it in money that was any good to us. What a basis for the stability of Canadian agriculture! What a hoax it is for the government to represent such a policy as one of stability for Canada's basic industry!
The house may be interested to know that in order to supply her needs Britain at times had to pay much higher prices to others than to us. As the minister said, in some cases she was able to get some goods at less. At one time, however, when the Canadian government was selling cheese to Britain at twenty-five cents a pound Britain purchased certain quantities from the United States and had to pay forty-seven cents a pound for it.
Agricultural Products Act

It is reported also that at a time when the Canadian government was selling our beef to Britain at twenty-two cents a pound, certain purchases were made by that country from the United States at thirty-three cents a pound. These were not large quantities, but they indicated the need in Great Britain and the prices prevailing elsewhere.
My third point is that the government itself has but little faith in this act. The government did not carry out the contracts it entered into.
Let me read from one contract, namely the bacon contract for this year of 1947. It states:
The British ministry of food undertakes to purchase and the Canadian government through the Canadian meat board undertakes to supply not less than 350 million pounds of Canadian bacon and ham during the calendar year of 1947
And a little farther down-[DOT]
The price payable by the ministry of food for such hams and bacon shall be as specified in article 2(a).
Then article 2 (a) reads as follows:
The following prices in Canadian funds per 100 pounds f.o.b. Canadian seaboard will apply in respect of bacon and hams supplied under this agreement. The price of Wiltshires grade A 45/80 pounds shall be $25 per 100 pounds f.o.b. Canadian seaboard.
Now, let me read the amounts that were delivered under these and other contracts. The minister provided this information in an answer to a question I asked a few days ago. Here are some of the things it tells us. With respect to bacon and hams the contract was for 350,000,000 pounds. The amount the government estimates will have been delivered at the end of the year will be 250,000,000 pounds, or about two-thirds. With respect to beef, the contract was for 120,000,000 pounds, and the government estimates that only 36,487,775 pounds will have been delivered by the end of this year. With respect to mutton and lamb the contract was for 10,000,000 pounds, and the government estimates that only something over 2,000,000 pounds will have been delivered by the end of this year, or about one-fifth of the contract. With respect to cheese the contract was for 125,000,000 pounds, and the government estimates that at the end of this year it will have delivered something over 57,000,000 pounds, or less than one-half of the total. In a few of the smaller contracts, namely in respect of evaporated milk, roller dried skim milk powder, and eggs, the full amount was delivered. But in respect of the major contracts, the amounts specified in the contract were not delivered.

My fourth point is that other policies of the government may well render the British contracts valueless. These British contracts are no good to farmers unless the prices are adequate and unless Britain is put in a position to pay for the goods this government sells her; and Britain cannot pay in full unless Canada continues to lend her money, or to buy more of her goods. And Canada has announced, through the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) that the government will not lend her any more money, and we all know we are not taking enough of her goods.
Let me read the statement of the Minister of Finance as it appeared in the local press on October 11, on his return from London. This is what he is reported to have said:
Under present conditions Canada's loan to Britain will last for another 12 to 14 months, and the Canadian government for the time being cannot see any possibility of extending further credits to Britain or any other country.
And a little farther down:
I told them that the $2 billion credit we had already extended to the United Kingdom ami Europe was all the Canadian economy could stand.
One could go on; but these are typical extracts from the speech of the Minister of Finance as reported on that day. It is by actions such as this that the government has removed1 from this legislation any basis of stability for our agriculture that these contracts ever had.
Let me point out now some bad effects of this measure and the way in which it has been administered.
First, this policy does nothing to correct the dollar crisis. Sales under this act are all made in the sterling area; I think all of them to Great Britain. Yet we have been called here to an emergency session because of a crisis arising from our unfavourable balance of trade with the United States; and the government continues to make that emergency worse by denying sales to that country.
The second bad result is this, that this policy, on the face of it, deceives our best customer, the United Kingdom. I have already read parts of one contract. It, and others, call for definite amounts to be delivered. I have also read a summary of the amounts delivered. These have shown that most contracts were not filled; on nearly all of them the government failed to deliver the amounts it agreed to deliver. There may have been some understanding between the two governments that these amounts would not be delivered; but what does the contract amount to if figures are put in there and then not lived up to?

Agricultural Products Act
The third bad result is that this measure is lessening Canada's production, and at a time when the world is short of food and particularly short of livestock products.
The number of hogs on farms in Canada in 1943 was 4,968,000; in 1946 it had dropped to 1,771,000. In respect of meat, total dressed and inspected, in 1943 the amount produced was 2.200 million pounds, while in 1947 it was only 1.290 million pounds. Cheese production in 1942 was 207,000,000 pounds, w'hile in 1947 it was only 118,000,000. Eggs produced in 1945 totalled 395,000,000 dozen. Production is still high, but it is falling. It has been held1 up by artificial props which were taken away by the action by the government on October 21 last. Then, in respect of oats, one of the coarse grains used in the production of livestock, we find that in 1943 there were 15-4 million acres sown, while in 1947 only 11-1 million acres were sown; and the same applies to barley', where we find that in 1943 there were 8-4 million acres sown and in 1947 only 7 million acres sown.
This is what the government policy has done to the basic industry of this country. This is what it has done at a time when there is the highest demand for agricultural products in the world's history.
It is said we have a scarcity of dollars, but the dollar area as well as the sterling area clamour for our food1 products of all kinds. Yet the government discourages and restrains farmers from maintaining production; and then it prevents the farmer from selling in an area where the much talked about dollars could be obtained. Is it any wonder we have come to a crisis.
The government calls it a dollar crisis. What it is, Mr. Speaker, is a production and a trade crisis which has been made worse by the government's interference with the normal course of production and trade.
The fourth result of this policy is that it has put Canadian agriculture into a strait-jacket. Following recent changes, it is driving the livestock industry into bankruptcy. It has done this, first, by preventing sales to the United States; second, by offering our products at relatively low prices to Britain and, third, by letting the farmers' costs rise unduly. The result has been a rising tide of anger all across the nation, a total lack of faith in government planning and a complete loss of confidence in the future of every branch of the livestock industry. The government's present, policy is open to no other interpretation than that the government means to cut down or liquidate the livestock industry in Canada.
In my judgment, the government deserves serious criticism, not only for certain provisions in the act itself, not only for faulty administration of the act, not only for the bad results flowing from it, the government also deserves censure for misrepresenting this and other plans as a stability program for Canadian agriculture.
Let me ask three simple questions. First, is dependence on sales to Britain, in the economic plight she is now in, a sound basis for stability for Canadian agriculture. The second question is this: Is dependence on sales to any country that cannot pay us for what we sell them unless we lend them the money a sound basis for stability of Canadian agriculture? It is a wholly absurd assumption.
In the fall of 1945 the government made a loan to Great Britain of the huge sum of $1,250 million. The Minister of Finance stated recently that there had been total loans of more than $2,000 million. Yet the government bases its whole program of stability for agriculture on sales to a country which, however, much we may regret it, has not the means to pay for the products w!e supply. Let us help her get the means to pay, but do not let us call it a stability plan for Canadian, agriculture when she cannot pay.
My third question is this: Since this policy of basing agricultural stability on these contracts is so infirm and unstable and since it can be carried out only by making huge loans to Britain and others to pay for what we sell them, where is the stability to the farming industry if the government discontinues such loans? And this the government has said it was doing-discontinuing the loans.
The government's policy in these matters is one of arbitrarily fixing certain farm prices at too low a level in relation to increasing costs. It is one of letting farm costs rise to a point where there is no profit in many lines of farm production. It is one of basing farm price stability on sales that can be paid for only if Canada continues to lend the money, and the government has said that it would not lend any more money. To call that a stability program is just another attempt by the government's propaganda machine to justify an inadequate policy by giving it a respectable name.
The functioning of this act has been possible only because of government loans and taxpayers' subsidies, by discontinuing the making of new loans and the payment of subsidies the government has cut the props from under it. The program has failed to meet the promises made for it. Three weeks of discussion between the two governments without
522
Agricultural Products Act

definite results have demonstrated that. The contracts are in a chaotic state and the new proposals announced today are but an exposition of the futility of the plan. They patch it up a bit but offer no substantial improvement. Canadian agriculture is in its present plight because the government has failed in these and other attempts by bureaucratic administration to run the farmers' business.
The farm situation today is an example, not of how planned stability can be brought about, but of how planned chaos is achieved. And the government is entirely responsible for it. The government took upon itself the power to fix prices for farm products, to subsidize farm products and to desubsidize them, to interfere with the farmers' ordinary market, to requisition products for export and to advise farmers by printed bulletins and over the radio to follow courses which proved to be unwise. In brief, the government told the farmers it was going to guide agriculture so as to bring them into the promised land of stability. The result is that the farmers have no confidence in the government's policy, nor have they any confidence in the government's capacity to plan by this measure for agriculture. They feel that they have been sold down the river. The results have proved that no good can come to the Canadian farmer by the minister being invested with these wide powers.
Amidst all this there are two points we should ever keep in mind. The first is that legislation of this kind, with all its weaknesses, will not save the British market to us. More constructive steps than this must be taken to that end. The second is that this legislation, whatever else it does, has one major defect, and that is to keep farm prices down at a time when farm costs are rising and farm production down at a time when the world is short of food.
Canada is dependent for her prosperity on export markets. That being the case, we in this party stand for a free market economy. We stand for the immediate removal of export embargoes on farm products-embargoes which are restricting the production of food. Why should the government be asking for freer access to the United States market for a hundred different products and yet deny to farmers the right to sell in that market? We ask that the government immediately discontinue its present policy of marketing the farmers' products below market prices and below production costs.
We call for an end to the confusion and deception about ceiling and floor prices. To suggest that the government is going to all

this trouble to provide floor prices when there is the greatest demand for food the world has ever known is sheer nonsense. Floor prices are needed when- demand is low and we have provision for that in several statutes. The government's policy has kept farm prices down in relation to other prices and has done so practically ever since it has been in office.
For the long term we stand for such subsidies as have already been authorized by the government in existing legislation, such as the Farm Prices Support Act, the Fisheries Prices Support Act and the Canadian Wheat Board Act. And if we are to protect the farmer against low prices, as the government has already done for wheat, we must also be prepared when necessary to protect the consumer against abnormally high prices for bread.
We are opposed to the government's present policy of loading the major burden of its price control policy on one section of the people. The government's price control policy in this and other measures is to keep farm prices down. In relation to present conditions it throws our whole economy out of balance. We must arrive at a balanced position in this matter. Workers and farmers and business and industry must all be treated equitably, no one being singled out for favours. And where protection against the cost of the essentials of life has to be provided for those in the low income groups, the nation as a whole should bear it.
We should have no controls that limit production. Farmers should be encouraged to produce. They should have the stimulus of good prices which their competitors in neighbouring countries have.
Let us apply the floor price legislation when floors are needed. We already have measures for this on the statute books; they are in permanent form.
No, Mr. Speaker, this plan of the government is not an expansion plan. It is but another instalment of the government's austerity program. The emergency exchange control bill which we discussed two days ago is one side of their coin; this is the other side of the same coin.
By the government's recent moves the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) has been given power to put business and industry into a strait-jacket. By this act the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is being given power to put agriculture into a strait-jacket.
These agreements up to date have resulted in a heavy loss to the agricultural industry. The over-all result on the Canadian economy will be depressed standards of living for the people of Canada as a whole. We are, there-

Agricultural Products Act
fore, opposed to this resolution. We do not propose to leave the minister in a position to continue to exploit the farmers of Canada, while he gambles with the price levels, nor do we intend to support a measure which leads only to lessened production at a time when the world is short of food.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, though I shall have critical remarks to make of the minister's administration of the Department of Agriculture before I am through, I can hardly conceive that the members of this house would oppose the continuance of the objectives of this "legislation to enable the government to fulfil its obligations under the British agreements, to export food supplies for the relief of the suffering and continue the distribution of essential foodstuffs in order to ensure stability to our agriculture and an orderly transition from war to peace."
The farmers of this country will be interested in reading the remarks of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken). However critical they may be of government policy, the majority of our farmers do not want to return to a free market economy whereby they might, it is true, be able to take advantage for a limited period of a short supply of foodstuffs but later on would be at the mercy of the wolves in the years that lie ahead.
The chief criticism has been that the farmers have been compelled to sell their products at a price which has been less than the cost of production, while this government has removed controls and allowed farm machinery, binder twine, fertilizer and all the other products which the farmer is compelled to use in his production, to skyrocket in price. That has placed the farmer in an impossible position.
On October 21 last, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) paid a visit to the town in which I live, Sturgis, Saskatchewan; and I was in the audience at a meeting which the minister addressed. A large number of people came from long distances to hear him, and one of my good supporters said to me after the meeting, " Mr. Gardiner has won a great many supporters tonight." The minister told the audience of his trip to Europe and something of the food situation there and of the struggle he was having to prevent speculators from reaping fortunes at the expense of the producers. He did not mention the C.C.F. in the hour that he spoke.
Within forty-eight hours the removal of the ceilings on coarse grains was announced, and I saw this C.C.F. supporter, who said, " I take back all I said the other night." He said a great many other things which I would not be allowed to put on the record. Those who heard the Minister of Agriculture that night 5849-34i
felt that he had really let them down by presenting the sort of argument he did tonight in concluding his remarks, and then being a party to placing the farmers in a position where those who sold their grain lost sums of money they could not afford to lose, and placing speculators in a position where they were able to make sums of money they did not deserve.
Since I heard the Minister of Agriculture speak on October 21 last, I have been in eight of the nine provinces of Canada; and wherever I was, whether it was in the Fraser Valley or in Prince Edward Island, or in Saskatchewan, I found that the farmers felt that the minister's action had been a very severe blow to them. They felt that they had made real sacrifices during the war in increasing their production when they were short of manpower and knew that they were not getting a fair share of the national income. They knew that all war contracts were awarded on a cost-plus basis; but they knew that the production of wheat, bacon and' beef was financed on a cost-minus basis, and they felt that some day they would be given a chance to get some adjustment made. They certainly did not expect to be treated in this way. Many of them had sold all their coarse grains.
The president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture summed up the views of the farmers when he addressed the dominion-provincial conference on agriculture at the Chateau Laurier in Ottawa on December 3. Mr. Hannam then said:
There is an atmosphere of uncertainty pervading this conference.
And again:
The uncertainty and bewilderment evident here is much the same as that which every farmer in Canada feels.
He went on to say:
I have never known a time when all livestock farmers, including dairy and poultry producers. were so upset, so discouraged, so bewildered. *
I frankly admit that I felt the same way today, although the Minister of Agriculture took occasion to attempt to reassure us.

Mr. Speaker, I rise only to tell a short story. That story is about a medical experiment which concerns an animal, namely a dog. The experiment is simply this. A dog was placed in confinement in a small room, and the doctors undertook to shine a square of light on the floor of this room at a certain time. Immediately after the square of light was shone on the floor of this room, the dog was fed; and the dog was happy. At another time in the day they shone an oblong of light on the floor of the dog's confinement cell and the dog was beaten; he was beaten gently, but he was beaten. In time this dog understood that when the square of light appeared on the floor he would be fed and that when the oblong of light appeared on the floor he would be beaten; and he was a happy dog. Then the scientists undertook to contract the oblong of light until it approached the proportions of a square. The dog, who understood he would be fed when there was a square of light and beaten when there was an oblong of light, was a completely happy dog; and he knew the situation. But as the oblong of light approached proportions of a square of light, the dog began to be confused; and in the end, as the oblong of light became almost coincident with the square of light, the dog suffered a nervous breakdown.
That is only a small illustration of uncertainty. The dog who was sure when he knew what his fate was, was a happy dog. He did not mind whether he was beaten or whether he was fed; he was certain of his future. I cite this small story, which is a true scientific story, only to illustrate the situation in which the farmers of the country find themselves today. I come from an urban constituency. The answer given by the Minister of Finance was this:
I shall take note of my hon. friend's question, as he did not give me any notice of it. May I say that the embargoes contained in the bill now- before the house do not materially affect exports from the United Kingdom.
I refer to that only for this reason. We were told during the debate on the extension of the Agricultural Products Act that one means by which Great Britain will be able to pay the increased prices which we are asking for our agricultural products-incidentally those increased prices have not been communicated to the house-is through the British people being able to export more of their manufactured products to Canada. speechtext:
Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution.
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to make provision for the making of emergency payments by the Minister of Mines and Resources to assist in meeting the increased cost of production of gold produced from gold mines during the three years commencing on December 1, 1947.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EMERGENCY PAYMENTS TO ASSIST IN MEETING INCREASED COST OF PRODUCTION
speechtext:
There is no such intention. In moving this resolution, Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to make any extended statement. I shall avoid any argument and confine myself to the giving of factual information which I am sure hon. members and the public would like to have at their disposal immediately.
As I indicated in replying to the leader of the opposition, I suggest that it would be desirable to let the resolution pass quickly in order that the bill may be introduced and made available to all members and the debate take place on second reading. With the unanimous consent of the house, it would, I believe, be possible to pass the resolution, give first reading to the bill, and begin debate on the second reading of the bill today. This would provide an opportunity for those hon. members who are particularly interested to speak on the bill with the bill itself before them.
There is, as I have indicated, little that I wish or need to say at this time. On December 11 last, at page 194 of Hansard, I made a statement, outlining the terms on which it is proposed to make payments to gold mines in order to assist them in defraying part of the
Gold Mining

substantially increased costs of production, and giving the reasons which had led us to modify our original proposal. On that same day or the following day, certain statements which have a bearing on the problem were issued by others. For the convenience of members and with the consent of the house, I should like to place on Hansard at the close of my remarks copies of the two statements issued by the international monetary fund on December 11, 1947, the first outlining the fund's policy with regard to gold mining subsidies generally, and the second dealing specifically with the revised Canadian proposal and the statement issued by the national advisory council of the United States government under date of December 12, 1947. As the house knows, the national advisory council is made up of the secretary of the treasury, the secretary of state, the secretary of commerce, the chairman of the board of governors of the federal reserve system, and the chairman of the board of directors of the export-import bank of Washington.
It will be recalled that for a period of three years beginning December 1, 1947, we propose to make payments through the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen) to the operators of gold mines on the following basis. The first step in the calculation is to take half of the amount by which a mine's cost of producing an ounce of gold in the year of payment exceeds $18 per ounce. Having obtained this basic rate of assistance in the case of the particular mine, it is applied to the amount by which production in the current year exceeds two-thirdis of production in the base year, which is the twelve months' period ending June 30, 1947. In the case of new mines, the payment as described above will be paid on the entire production in the first year, and in the two succeeding years on the amount by which current production exceeds two-thirds of the first year's production.
Since the announcement was made, considerable interest has been expressed in the items that would be included in cost of production. I think it will help hon. members if I give them this information immediately.
In the new bill, "cost of production" of gold from a mine during any period is defined as "the costs incurred by the operator of the mine in, and properly attributable to, the production of gold produced from the mine during that period, and includes mining, milling, smelting, refining, transportation and administrative costs so incurred and so attributable, and includes such amounts in respect of depreciation, amortization of pre-

production expenses, and costs of exploration and development in the mine as may be determined in accordance with the regulations, but does not include any amount in respect of depletion or off-property exploration and development, or, subject to the regulations, any amount not allowable as an expense or deduction in determining income from the mine for the purposes of the Income War Tax Act."
It will be noted that in this definition the attempt is made to provide for a reasonable determination of cost of production, including all items of cost that could be legitimately included for a purpose of this kind. Depletion, off-property exploration and development and any amount not allowable as an expense or deduction for income tax purpose are not allowed, but depreciation, amortization of preproduction expenses, and1 costs of exploration and development in the mine are allowed in reasonable amounts to be determined by regulation. It is the intention that the regulations will provide for determining an allowable amount of mine exploratory and development expense on the basis of the historical experience of the mine-say, the average for the period 1939-41-adjusted upward for recent increases in costs. In the case of new mines, it is expected that the amounts allowed will be determined by reference to the average allowed in the case of all old or established mines.
It will, of course, not be possible to determine with finality a mine's average cost of producing an ounce of gold during any payment year, until after the end of the year. However, power will be taken in the bill to prescribe by regulation the times at which amounts payable under the legislation may be made and to authorize the minister to make advances in respect of the payments to be made on the gold produced in any payment year. My hope would be that it would be possible to make interim payments, say, shortly after the end of each quarter, subject to final adjustment and determination after the end of the year.
The statements to which I referred and which I should like to place on Hansard are as follows:
Statement by the international monetary fund issued December 11, 1947
The international monetary fund has a responsibility to see that the gold policies of its members do not undermine or threaten to undermine exchange stability. Consequently, every member which proposes to introduce new measures to subsidize the production of gold is under obligation to consult with the fund on the specific measures to be introduced.
Under article IV, section 2. of the articles of agreement of the fund, members are prohibited

Gold Mining
from buying gold at a price above parity plus the prescribed margin. In the view of the fund a subsidy in the form of a uniform payment per ounce for all or part of the gold produced would constitute an increase in price which would not be permissible if the total price paid by the member for gold were thereby to become in excess of parity plus the prescribed margin. Subsidies involving payments in another form may also, depending upon their nature, constitute an increase in price.
Under article IV, section 4(a), each member of the fund "undertakes to collaborate with the fund to promote exchange stability, to maintain orderly exchange arrangements with other members. and to avoid competitive exchange alterations." Subsidies on gold production regardless of their form are inconsistent with article IV, section 4(a). if they undermine or threaten to undermine exchange stability. This would be the case for example if subsidies were to cast widespread doubt on the uniformity of the monetary value of gold in all member countries.
Subsidies which do not directly affect exchange stability may nevertheless contribute directly or indirectly to monetary instability in other countries and hence be of concern to the fund.
A determination by the fund that a proposed subsidy is not inconsistent with the foregoing principles will depend upon the circumstances in each case. Moreover, the fund may find that subsidies which are justified at any one time may, because of changing conditions and changing effects, later prove to be inconsistent with the foregoing principles. In order to carry out its objectives the fund will continue to study and to review with its members their gold policies and any proposed changes to determine if they are consonant with the provisions of the fund agreement and conducive to a sound international policy regarding gold.
Statement by the international monetary fund
issued on December 11. 1947, for release in morning papers of December 12, 1947
The Canadian government has consulted with the fund regarding its proposed gold production subsidy and has today made an announcement on this subject. The fund has examined the present Canadian proposal in the light of its own general statement of policy published today. The fund has determined that in the present circumstances the proposed Canadian action is not inconsistent with the policy stated by the fund.
Press Release by National Advisory Council
The United States government welcomes the statement of the international monetary fund respecting measures to subsidize the production of gold. The expressed intention of the fund to keep under review the gold policies of its members in the light of a sound international gold policy is an important forward step in the field of international financial co-operation.
The United States, as a gold-buying country, has a peculiar and continuing interest in the role which gold subsidies may come to play in the production, movement and price of gold. In particular, the United States would view with disfavour any tendencies for countries to become dependent on subsidized gold production as a solution to the problem of arriving at and maintaining equilibrium in the balance of international payments.
In the view of the council there are no grounds which would justify instituting a subsidy to encourage the production of gold in this country. The present gold stocks of the United States amount to no less than $22-7 billion. In the first eleven months of 1947 gold purchased by the United States from foreign countries amounted to $2-7 billion.
December 12, 1947.

I am pleased, Mr. Speaker, to see the house in a splendid Christmas mood.
I realize that the house is anxious to see this bill, but the proposal made by the minister involves a principle that we cannot let go without a statement. The principle of the bill embodies one of a bonus. It is a principle which we cannot approve. Even if it involved the payment of a large bonus per ounce on all gold production, and was likely to be a real help to the industry, I cannot aprove any one industry receiving a bounty at the hands of the Canadian taxpayer. Ardent supporter of gold mining as I am, I cannot and do not approve the industry becoming the ward of the state and in receipt of a public bounty.
What effect the bill would have-and that it will have any material beneficial and lasting effect is open to serious question- a better and more economically sound solution was available. The desperate plight of the gold mining industry is directly attributable to government action. This scheme of doubtful value is a straw to a drowning man. He may think it will save his life and therefore clutch at it as some members of the gold mining industry have done.
I do not propose at this time to enlarge on the suggestions I have already made to this house on the gold mining industry, and that gold should be allowed to benefit by a free and open market; nor do I propose to put on Hansard any of the elaborate and rather voluminous statements I have with regard to the ability of the open market to absorb the Canadian production; nor do I propose to make any statement with regard to my opposition to adherence to all the clauses of the international monetary fund; nor do I propose to say anything about the fictitious values placed on all currencies of the world by the international monetary fund, which are

6.	That on and after November 18, 1947, the excise tax of one per cent per pound on sugar, grape sugar, glucose, sugar syrup, corn syrup, etc., be repealed.

That the customs tariff be amended to provide:

speechtext: I move that the house do now adjourn.

Before that motion is put, may I ask the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance one question? It has to do with the government's proposal with respect to the loan of 8300,000,000 from the export-import bank? Will that require legislation? If so, what; and when will it be brought forward?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not in a position to give my hon. friend a definite answer now, but I think it will not require legislation. I think the borrowing authority which we now have is sufficient to enable us to do it. But if not, if it is exhausted-although I am not quite sure about it at the moment-we might have to come to the house for additional authority.
At the moment you have no plans for bringing in legislation with respect to that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. We will not bring it up, of course, if it is not necessary. If our borrowing authority is sufficient, we shall not need to; but if it is not, we shall. But that will be determined before the resumed session.

It likely will be needed by that time.
